propositions.text: The Minister appeals the RPD decision granting refugee status to a Georgian citizen.
propositions.quote: The Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness (the Minister) appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated February 1, 2018, that determined that the XXXX XXXX, citizen of Georgia, is a Convention refugee.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister appeals the RPD decision granting refugee status to a Georgian citizen, as stated by the court.

propositions.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's decision that the appellant is a Convention refugee under IRPA paragraph 111(1)(a).
propositions.quote: The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is a Convention refugee, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's refugee status decision under IRPA, as stated by the court.

propositions.text: The respondent is a 51-year-old Georgian woman granted refugee protection as a domestic violence victim.
propositions.quote: The Respondent is a fifty-one year old women from Georgia who was granted refugee protection as a victim of domestic violence.

propositions.text: She first tried to enter Canada in 2016 with a fraudulent Canadian passport but was turned back in Cuba before seizure in Germany.
propositions.quote: She first tried to travel to Canada in XXXX 2016 with a fraudulent Canadian passport, but was turned back in Cuba before the document was seized in Germany.

propositions.text: She succeeded in entering Canada the next month with a false passport and claimed asylum at the airport.
propositions.quote: She tried again to come to Canada with a false passport the following month. This time she was successful and was able to claim asylum at the airport upon her arrival.

propositions.text: The RPD found her testimony and documentary evidence internally consistent with no adverse credibility findings and likely true.
propositions.quote: The RPD concluded that her testimony and documentary evidence was internally consistent. No adverse credibility findings were made and the RPD concluded that her narrative is likely true.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent is a 51-year-old Georgian woman granted refugee protection; the RPD found her testimony credible and consistent, as stated by the court.

propositions.text: The respondent did not disclose her prior failed attempt to enter Canada with a false passport, discovered by CBSA database check.
propositions.quote: The Respondent did not disclose her previous failed attempt to come to Canada with a false passport under a different identity. This fact only came to light as the result of a database check conducted by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA).

propositions.text: The respondent admitted the allegation but explained nondisclosure was due to nervousness and fear.
propositions.quote: The Respondent admitted that the allegation is true, but explained that she did not disclose this information because she was nervous and afraid.

propositions.text: The Minister intervened, arguing the respondent should be excluded under article 1F(b) for a serious non-political crime before arrival.
propositions.quote: As a result of this discovery, the Minister intervened in writing on the basis the Respondent ought to be excluded from refugee protection by application of article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention as incorporated into the IRPA by section 98. The Minister argued that the Respondent's use of a fraudulent Canadian passport is a non-political crime committed before arrival in Canada that is sufficiently serious to warrant exclusion.

propositions.text: The RPD allowed the claim based on credibility and finding no crime was committed.
propositions.quote: The RPD allowed her claim for protection on the basis of credibility and a finding that a crime was not committed.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent did not disclose a prior false passport attempt; the Minister argued exclusion under article 1F(b); the RPD allowed the claim, as stated by the court.

propositions.text: The Minister objects to the RPD's decision on two grounds: legal error on article 1F(b) and failure to consider lack of truthfulness in credibility.
propositions.quote: The Minister objects to the RPD's positive determination on two grounds. First, the RPD erred in its interpretation and application of the law pertaining to article 1F(b) exclusion. Second, the RPD failed to take the Respondent's lack of truthfulness into account in finding that she is credible.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister objects to the RPD decision for legal error on article 1F(b) and ignoring lack of truthfulness in credibility, as submitted by the Minister.

propositions.text: The RAD standard of review is correctness unless deference is warranted due to RPD's meaningful advantage; no such issue identified.
propositions.quote: The standard of review for appeals to the RAD is that of correctness, unless deference should be shown to the RPD because it enjoyed a meaningful advantage over the RAD. No issue was identified to which deference should be shown on this basis.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD applies correctness standard of review unless deference is warranted; no deference issue identified, as stated by the court.

propositions.text: No new evidence or oral hearing request was filed; analysis begins on RPD's credibility determination.
propositions.quote: No new evidence was filed and no request was made for an oral hearing. ANALYSIS The RPD did not err in determining that the Respondent is credible

paragraphs.summary: No new evidence or hearing requested; analysis begins on RPD's credibility determination, as stated by the court.

propositions.text: The RPD applied Chairperson's Guideline 4 and considered psychiatric report, finding the respondent credible after reviewing evidence.
propositions.quote: The RPD applied Chairperson's Guideline 4, Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-related Persecution and took note of the psychiatric report. After reviewing the supporting documentation and oral testimony, the Respondent was found to be credible.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD applied Guideline 4 and psychiatric report, finding the respondent credible, as reported by the RPD.

propositions.text: The RPD considered Minister's submission on deliberate misleading but concluded respondent not excluded under article 1F(b).
propositions.quote: The panel noted the Minister's submission that the Respondent engaged in a deliberate attempt to mislead the RPD and that this should be taken into account in assessing credibility. The panel proceeded to conclude that the Respondent is not described in article 1F(b) of the Convention,

propositions.text: The RPD found no major concerns with evidence but failed to account for false passport documents in reasons.
propositions.quote: The RPD went on to say that it had no major or identifiable concerns with the evidence submitted, but failed to account for the documents pertaining to the false passport in its reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD considered Minister's submission but concluded no article 1F(b) exclusion; failed to address false passport documents in reasons, as reported by the RPD.

propositions.text: The RPD accepted respondent's testimony that false passport was used to claim asylum in Canada.
propositions.quote: First, the panel accepted the Respondent's testimony that she used it for the purpose of claiming asylum in Canada.

propositions.text: The RPD concluded that using the false passport while transiting does not show lack of subjective fear and found respondent credible on fear.
propositions.quote: Because she was proceeding to Canada through transit countries, the panel concluded that her conduct is not demonstrative of a lack of subjective fear. The RPD found her to be credible with respect to her subjective fear.

propositions.text: The RPD concluded the use of false passport is not an offence under section 133 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: The RPD then went on to conclude that her use of the false passport is not an offence by virtue of section 133 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD accepted the respondent's testimony on asylum claim, found no lack of subjective fear, and concluded no offence under IRPA section 133, as reported by the RPD.

propositions.text: There is a difference between fact findings and subjective fear assessment; the RPD confused these steps.
propositions.quote: There is a difference between findings of fact made on a balance of probabilities standard and an assessment of whether the facts, as determined, establish a lack of subjective fear. The RPD confused the two steps by assessing the credibility of a subjective fear.

propositions.text: The RPD accepted respondent's testimony as true and found evidence shows subjective fear.
propositions.quote: What the RPD appears to have meant was that the Respondent's testimony was accepted as being true, and that the evidence, as established, demonstrates a subjective fear of persecution.

propositions.text: The Minister submits the RPD failed to consider false passport use in credibility assessment, ignoring Minister's submission without reasons.
propositions.quote: As a result of this methodological error, the Minister is correct in submitting that the RPD failed to account for the use of the false passport in its credibility assessment, given that this only figures in its subjective fear analysis. The RPD ignored the Minister's submission about credibility without providing reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD confused fact and subjective fear assessments and ignored Minister's submission on false passport in credibility, as submitted by the Minister and found by the court.

propositions.text: Respondent's testimony is presumed true unless good reasons to doubt exist.
propositions.quote: The Respondent's testimony is presumed to be true unless there are good reasons to doubt it.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence is extensive and consistent; psychiatric report explains nondisclosure at port of entry due to fear and depression.
propositions.quote: I reviewed the documentary evidence filed and note that it is extensive, and includes supporting medical reports. Identity documents were attached to the supporting statements. Her testimony at the hearing was consistent. Although the psychiatric report can help assess her testimony that she did not disclose the truth about the previous use of a false passport, this allowance can only reasonably be extended to the port of entry. She testified that she was depressed and afraid.

propositions.text: Depression and fear do not explain failure to disclose false passport use to counsel for Basis of Claim; RPD erred in not drawing adverse credibility inference.
propositions.quote: However, the Respondent was represented by counsel when she drafted and filed the Basis of Claim (BOC). Depression and fear cannot reasonably account for her failure to disclose pertinent details to her lawyer for inclusion in the BOC. Her explanation does not adequately respond to the question of why she failed to disclose this information on her own accord, even after taking the psychiatric report into consideration. The RPD erred in failing to draw an adverse credibility inference from this and to include it in its credibility assessment.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds testimony presumed true; psychiatric report explains nondisclosure at entry but not to counsel; RPD erred by not drawing adverse credibility inference.

propositions.text: No other reliability issues found; oral testimony consistent and supported by evidence including medical reports.
propositions.quote: After reviewing the documentary evidence, I find no other problems that would put the reliability of testimony and documentary evidence into question. Her oral testimony was internally consistent and supported by a significant amount of reliable evidence, including medical reports.

propositions.text: Adverse inference from forged passport use insufficient to rebut presumption of truth; respondent likely truthful about mistreatment in Georgia.
propositions.quote: The adverse inference drawn from the use of the forged passport is insufficient to rebut the presumption of truth in this case. Although the RPD erred in its assessment of this issue, my independent assessment leads me to conclude that the Respondent is likely telling the truth about mistreatment in Georgia.

propositions.text: The RPD was correct in its conclusion despite errors in credibility evaluation.
propositions.quote: The RPD was correct in its conclusion, despite having erred in its evaluation of credibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no other reliability issues; adverse inference insufficient to rebut truth presumption; RPD's conclusion correct despite credibility errors.

propositions.text: Minister's Notice of Intervention alleges respondent committed crimes of personation and forged passport under Criminal Code sections 403 and 57.
propositions.quote: The Notice of Intervention filed by the Minister prior to the hearing alleges that the Respondent committed crimes that, if committed in Canada, would be offences under sections 403 and 57 of the Criminal Code of Canada (CCC). The first concerns personation that is punishable with imprisonment not exceeding ten years. The second concerns the use of a forged passport that can result in imprisonment for up to fourteen years.

propositions.text: Minister cites Febles Supreme Court decision to argue these offences are serious for article 1F(b) exclusion due to potential jail terms.
propositions.quote: The Minister cites the Febles decision of the Supreme Court of Canada to submit that these offences are serious for purposes of article 1F(b) exclusion because of the potential length of the jail terms.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister alleges crimes of personation and forged passport and cites Febles decision to argue seriousness for exclusion, as stated by the Minister.

propositions.text: Minister cites IRPA section 133 providing protection from charges under CCC sections 57 or 403 pending refugee claim outcome.
propositions.quote: The Minister then cites section 133 of the IRPA that provides that a person may not be charged with an offence under sections 57 or 403 of the CCC, pending the outcome of the refugee claim, if they came to Canada directly or indirectly from the country of alleged persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister cites IRPA section 133 protecting from charges under certain CCC offences pending refugee claim outcome, as stated by the Minister.

propositions.text: Minister relies on Uppal Federal Court decision that section 133 protects those using false passports to claim asylum in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Minister relied on the Uppal decision of the Federal Court to submit that section 133 affords protection from prosecution to those who use false passports in order to make their way to Canada to claim asylum.

propositions.text: Minister submits section 133 exception does not apply to respondent because first forged passport use was not related to current claim or arrival in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Minister submits that this exception does not apply to the Respondent because her use of the first forged passport did not take place in relation to her arrival in Canada in the course of her current claim for protection, nor does the evidence establish that she used the passport to claim asylum in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister relies on Uppal decision that section 133 protects false passport users claiming asylum, but submits it does not apply to respondent's first forged passport use.

propositions.text: The RPD reasoned respondent would have benefited from section 133 exemption if she had reached Canada with first false passport.
propositions.quote: The panel reasoned that the Respondent would have made it to Canada with the false Canadian passport if she had not been turned back in Cuba. Consequently, she would have benefited from the section 133 exemption if she had not been intercepted en route to Canada and returned to Georgia.

propositions.text: The RPD found same legal principle applied as when respondent arrived with false Slovakian passport and was not prosecuted due to section 133.
propositions.quote: The legal principle is the same as was the case when she arrived in Canada with a false Slovakian passport and was not prosecuted because of the operation of section 133.

propositions.text: The RPD declined to exclude respondent on basis she did not commit a crime before entering Canada.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the RPD declined to exclude the Respondent on the basis that she did not commit a crime before entering Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found respondent would have benefited from section 133 if she reached Canada with first false passport and declined exclusion for no crime before entry, as reported by the RPD.

propositions.text: Minister objects that section 133 does not apply as respondent did not reach Canada with first forged passport, citing Uppal and Kathirgamathamby.
propositions.quote: The Minister objects to this decision for the following reasons. First, the section 133 exemption is not applicable because the Respondent was not successful in reaching Canada with the first forged passport. The Minister again cites Uppal in support of the submission that the exception only applies to those who use false travel documents in order to enter Canada. The Minister also cites the Federal Court Kathirgamathamby decision, in which the section 133 exception was not extended to a person who used a forged passport to enter the United States because the exception only applies if the fraudulent document was used to enter Canada.

propositions.text: Minister cites Ontario courts' Mossavat decisions supporting interpretation that section 133 exemption restricts to physical entry into Canada.
propositions.quote: The Ontario Court of Justice and Ontario Court of Appeal Mossavat decisions are cited in support of the proposition that the correct statutory interpretation of section 133 restricts the exemption to those who enter Canada physically.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister objects that section 133 exemption does not apply as respondent did not reach Canada with first forged passport, citing Uppal, Kathirgamathamby, and Mossavat decisions, as submitted by the Minister.

propositions.text: Minister submits RPD erred in law by applying section 133 retroactively; Parliament did not intend protection for past offences unrelated to entry.
propositions.quote: The Minister submits that the RPD erred in law when it found that the exception would have applied if she had arrived in Canada. Section 133 cannot be used retroactively, as the panel believed that it could. Parliament did not intend to extend this protection to offences relating to forged travel documents that occurred at any time and in any place in the past. To do so would undermine the purpose of article 1F(b) exclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister submits the RPD erred by applying section 133 retroactively; Parliament did not intend protection for past offences unrelated to entry, as submitted by the Minister.

propositions.text: Respondent submits Minister's interpretation of section 133 conflicts with refugee law principles and Canada's human rights commitments.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that the Minister's interpretation of section 133 is incompatible with the principles of refugee law and with Canada's international human rights commitments.

propositions.text: Respondent argues use of first passport was solely to seek asylum; failure to arrive does not change purpose of use.
propositions.quote: She used the first passport for no other reason than to seek asylum in Canada. Her failure to arrive in Canada does not alter the purpose with which she used the passport.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent submits the Minister's section 133 interpretation conflicts with refugee law and human rights; use of first passport was solely to seek asylum, as submitted by the respondent.

propositions.text: The Respondent distinguishes Uppal because it involved a fraudulent driver's licence not used to enter Canada.
propositions.quote: The Respondent distinguishes the Uppal decision because that case concerned the use of a fraudulent driver's licence that was not used to gain admission to Canada.

propositions.text: The court found the passport was entitled to section 133 exemption in Uppal.
propositions.quote: Of note is the fact that the court found that the passport was entitled to the benefit of the section 133 exemption.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent distinguishes Uppal as it involved a fraudulent driver's licence not used to enter Canada, noting the passport was exempt under section 133.

propositions.text: Respondent distinguishes Kathirgamathamby because it involved a false passport used to enter the US, not Canada, and no asylum intent in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Respondent also distinguishes the Kathirgamathamby decision from the facts of the appeal. This case concerned a person who used a false passport to enter the United States. Although he came to Canada to claim asylum after he was released from detention, he never stated that he used the fraudulent travel document with the intention of seeking asylum in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent distinguishes Kathirgamathamby as it involved false passport use to enter the US, not Canada, and no asylum intent in Canada.

propositions.text: Section 133 concerns the purpose of travel, not success in reaching Canada; Respondent used fraudulent passport solely to seek asylum in Canada, so section 133 applies.
propositions.quote: The Respondent submits that section 133 concerns the purpose of the travel, not whether or not the person was successful in reaching Canada. Because the Respondent used the first fraudulent passport for the sole purpose of seeking asylum in Canada, section 133 applies.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues section 133 focuses on travel purpose, not arrival success; Respondent used fraudulent passport solely to seek asylum, so section 133 applies.

propositions.text: Section 133 must be interpreted in light of Canada's international human rights obligations to avoid absurd results excluding asylum seekers who used fraudulent documents.
propositions.quote: The Respondent cites principles of statutory interpretation in support of the submission that section 133 must be interpreted in light of Canada's international human rights obligations.6 Exclusion of a person who used a fraudulent travel document to seek refugee protection in Canada because the trip was not successful would lead to an absurd result that is inconsistent with international human rights law and with the objectives of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Section 133's intent is to ensure asylum seekers are not prosecuted for using fraudulent documents to seek asylum in Canada.
propositions.quote: The intent of section 133 was to ensure that those who seek asylum in Canada are not prosecuted for using fraudulent documents to do so.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues section 133 must be interpreted with Canada's human rights obligations to avoid absurd exclusions; its intent is to protect asylum seekers from prosecution for fraudulent documents.

propositions.text: Article 1F(b) analysis must consider offence seriousness; Federal Court Tabagua supports that first use of false travel document here is not serious for exclusion.
propositions.quote: The Respondent goes on to submit that an article 1F(b) analysis must consider the seriousness of the offence.7 The Federal Court Tabagua decision is cited in support to the submission that, even if the section 133 exception did not apply, the first use of a false travel document under these circumstances should not be considered to be serious for purposes of exclusion from refugee protection.

propositions.text: The RPD did not err in declining to exclude the Respondent.
propositions.quote: The RPD did not err in declining to exclude the Respondent

paragraphs.summary: Respondent submits article 1F(b) requires considering offence seriousness; Tabagua supports first false document use here is not serious; RPD did not err in declining exclusion.

propositions.text: IRPA is remedial; statute must be interpreted fairly, liberally, avoiding absurd or unreasonable results.
propositions.quote: The Interpretation Act (the Act) deems the IRPA to be remedial in nature. In order to achieve this result, consideration of the Act's objectives needs to be done in the context of a "fair, large and liberal construction" of the statute.

propositions.text: Legislature presumed not to intend absurd, illogical, or incompatible interpretations with Act's object.
propositions.quote: The legislature is presumed not to intend absurd, ridiculous or frivolous consequences, nor an interpretation that is extremely unreasonably, inequitable, illogical, incoherent or incompatible with other provisions of the Act or with the object of the legislative enactment.

propositions.text: Statutes must be read in context, grammatical and ordinary sense, harmoniously with scheme, object, and Parliament's intention.
propositions.quote: Today there is only one principle or approach, namely, the words of an Act are to be read in their entire context and in their grammatical and ordinary sense harmoniously with the scheme of the Act, the object of the Act, and the intention of Parliament.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues IRPA is remedial and must be interpreted fairly and contextually, avoiding absurd or illogical results, citing statutory interpretation principles.

propositions.text: Supreme Court of Canada calls this approach 'contextual and purposive' in interpreting IRPA transitional provisions.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court of Canada has also referred to this approach as being "contextual and purposive."12

propositions.text: Court considered IRPA's purpose in interpreting appeal rights' transitional provisions.
propositions.quote: The Court specifically considered the purpose of the IRPA in interpreting its transitional provisions with respect to appeal rights.13

paragraphs.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada calls the approach 'contextual and purposive' and considered IRPA's purpose in interpreting appeal rights' transitional provisions.

propositions.text: Uppal decision concerns ID Admissibility Hearing about false passport and driver's licence use to enter Canada.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court Uppal decision concerns an Immigration Division (ID) Admissibility Hearing about whether the person concerned committed a crime by entering Canada with a false passport and driver's licence to make a refugee claim.

propositions.text: ID found individual not inadmissible for false passport due to section 133, but protection excluded driver's licence.
propositions.quote: The ID concluded that the individual is not inadmissible for having come to Canada with a false passport because of section 133, but that this protection does not extend to the driver's licence.

propositions.text: Submission argued section 133 protection for passports should extend to driver's licences by purposive interpretation.
propositions.quote: The Court rejected the submission that protection from prosecution afforded by section 133 to passports should be extended to driver's licences on the basis of principles of purposive statutory interpretation.

propositions.text: Court rejected extension of section 133 protection to driver's licences and upheld ID's determination.
propositions.quote: The Court rejected this argument and upheld the ID's determination.

propositions.text: Section 133 protects documents related to coming into Canada, sheltering bona fide refugees using false passports to enter Canada.
propositions.quote: On a plain reading of the provision, the protection extends to documents "in relation to the coming into Canada of the person". The intent is to allow bona fide refugees and refugee claimants to use false passports and supporting documents obtained by them for the purpose of making their way into Canada and to shelter them from a finding of inadmissibility for holding and using those documents.

propositions.text: ID correctly held protection applies only to fraudulent documents obtained for entering Canada.
propositions.quote: In examining the question of inadmissibility, the ID determined that an individual could be sheltered from a finding of inadmissibility only in relation to a fraudulent document that was obtained for the purpose of entering Canada. In my view, that interpretation is correct.

paragraphs.summary: The Uppal decision concerns an ID hearing on false passport and driver's licence; court upheld ID's finding that section 133 protects only documents used to enter Canada, not driver's licences.

propositions.text: Court considered IRPA's public safety and criminality objectives before limiting section 133 protection.
propositions.quote: The court considered the objectives of IRPA pertaining to public safety and criminality before concluding that section 133 cannot be extended to prevent prosecution for offences that were committed "for purposes wholly unrelated to fleeing persecution, to enter Canada."14

propositions.text: Section 133 does not prevent prosecution for fraudulent driver's licence use unrelated to asylum in Canada.
propositions.quote: For this reason, section 133 does not prevent prosecution in the case of the use of a fraudulent driver's licence for a number of years in the United Kingdom unrelated to seeking asylum in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court found section 133 cannot prevent prosecution for offences unrelated to fleeing persecution to enter Canada, such as fraudulent driver's licence use in the UK.

propositions.text: Kathirgamathamby decision involved US fraud conviction for forged passport and Canadian permanent residency rejection.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court Kathirgamathamby decision concerned a fraud conviction in the United States for having entered with country with a forged passport.15 After coming to Canada, his application for permanent residency was rejected on the grounds that the previous conviction rendered him inadmissible.

propositions.text: Court allowed judicial review due to flawed equivalency analysis in permanent residency rejection.
propositions.quote: The Court allowed the judicial review application on the basis that the equivalency analysis was seriously flawed.

propositions.text: Court obiter dictum relied on Uppal to say section 133 protection wouldn't apply if passport used to enter US, not Canada.
propositions.quote: By way of obiter dictum, the Court relied on Uppal in stating that section 133 protection would not have applied because the passport in question was used to enter the United States, not Canada.

propositions.text: Section 133 shields inadmissibility only if document used to enter Canada.
propositions.quote: At paragraph 17 the Court notes that this section "could shield a person from a finding of inadmissibility only if the document was used for the purpose of entering Canada."

propositions.text: Neither Uppal nor Kathirgamathamby dealt with prosecution in another country while in transit to Canada to claim asylum.
propositions.quote: Neither of the cases dealt with the situation of a person prosecuted in another country while in transit to Canada to claim asylum.

propositions.text: Kathirgamathamby concerns inadmissibility for foreign offence outside Canada unrelated to travel to claim asylum.
propositions.quote: The Kathirgamathamby case concerns paragraph 36(1)(b) inadmissibility for having been convicted of a foreign offence outside of Canada outside the context of travel to Canada to make a refugee claim.

propositions.text: Uppal and Kathirgamathamby are distinguishable from the case on appeal.
propositions.quote: As a result, the two cases are distinguishable from the case on appeal.

paragraphs.summary: Kathirgamathamby involved US fraud conviction and inadmissibility; court allowed review for flawed analysis; obiter dictum said section 133 applies only if document used to enter Canada; cases differ from current appeal.

propositions.text: Bellevue case considered Kathirgamathamby and found its comments on section 133 are non-binding obiter dictum.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court considered the Kathirgamathamby decision more recently in the Bellevue case and concluded that the comments pertaining to section 133 constitute non-binding obiter dictum.16

propositions.text: Bellevue concerned ID admissibility hearing on US conviction for fraudulent passport used to seek asylum in US.
propositions.quote: This case concerned an admissibility hearing conducted by the ID based on a conviction in the United States for use of a fraudulent passport that was said to have been used to seek asylum in that country.

propositions.text: ID applied Kathirgamathamby reasoning to conclude section 133 immunity does not apply if person never entered Canada.
propositions.quote: The ID applied the Court's reasoning in the Kathirgamathamby decision in concluding that section 133 immunity does not apply because the person concerned never entered Canada, even if it were true that a false document was used to enter the U.S. to claim asylum.

propositions.text: Court held ID erred in treating Kathirgamathamby comments as binding stare decisis; they are obiter dictum.
propositions.quote: The Court held that the ID erred in concluding that it was bound by principles of stare decisis because the Court's comments constitute obiter dictum that are not part of the binding ratio decidendi of the decision.

propositions.text: ID erred by excluding section 133 immunity in equivalency analysis.
propositions.quote: As a result, the ID committed a reviewable error in failing to include the applicability of section 133 immunity it its equivalency analysis of Canadian law.

paragraphs.summary: Bellevue case found Kathirgamathamby comments on section 133 are obiter dictum; ID erred by excluding section 133 immunity in equivalency analysis.

propositions.text: Uppal is not on point as it concerned fraudulent driver's licence unrelated to seeking asylum in Canada.
propositions.quote: The Uppal decision is not on point because it concerned the use of a fraudulent driver's licence unrelated to seeking asylum in Canada.

propositions.text: Kathirgamathamby did not concern travel to Canada to claim asylum and is not binding under stare decisis.
propositions.quote: The Kathirgamathamby case did not concern travel to Canada to claim asylum and is not binding in accordance with principles of stare decisis.

propositions.text: Section 133 immunity could apply if fraudulent travel document was used for entering Canada.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Court opined that section 133 immunity from prosecution could apply in circumstances in which the fraudulent travel document was used "for purposes of entering Canada."

propositions.text: Purpose of obtaining and using travel document before arriving in Canada is relevant for section 133 assessment.
propositions.quote: In the context of admissibility or prosecution, the purpose for which one obtained and used the travel document before physically arriving in Canada is a relevant consideration for a section 133 assessment.

propositions.text: Legal issue concerns immunity from prosecution for past crime, not a defense entitling acquittal.
propositions.quote: However, the legal issue concerns immunity from prosecution for a past crime, not whether section 133 acts as a defense that entitles one to an acquittal.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Uppal and Kathirgamathamby not binding; section 133 immunity may apply if document used to enter Canada; issue is immunity, not acquittal.

propositions.text: Section 133 jurisprudence concerns immunity from prosecution in Canada for fraudulent travel documents used to claim asylum.
propositions.quote: Section 133 jurisprudence concerns immunity from prosecution in Canada for the use of fraudulent document to travel to and enter to claim asylum.

propositions.text: Article 1F(b) exclusion is international criminal law applied in refugee law context.
propositions.quote: Article 1F(b) exclusion is a matter of international criminal law as applied in the context of refugee law.

propositions.text: Immunities from prosecution are mitigating factors for offence seriousness, not defenses negating offence.
propositions.quote: Immunities from prosecution are appropriately dealt with as mitigating factors for purposes of determining the seriousness of the offence, not as a defence that leads to the conclusion that no offence was committed.

paragraphs.summary: Court states section 133 concerns immunity from prosecution; Article 1F(b) is international criminal law; immunities mitigate offence seriousness, not negate offence.

propositions.text: IRPA refugee provisions incorporate international convention to which Canada is party.
propositions.quote: The refugee protection provisions of the IRPA incorporate an international convention to which Canada is a State party.

propositions.text: Vienna Convention Article 32 allows supplementary treaty interpretation means if wording is ambiguous or absurd.
propositions.quote: Article 32 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties provides that recourse may be made to supplementary means of interpreting treaty obligations, including preparatory work of the treaty and the circumstances of its conclusion, in cases where the wording of the treaty is ambiguous or obscure, or if a possible interpretation would lead to a result that is manifestly absurd or unreasonable.17

propositions.text: Vienna Convention Article 31 requires treaties be interpreted in good faith in light of context, object and purpose.
propositions.quote: Article 31 of the Convention requires that treaties be "interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to the terms of the treaty in the context and in the light of its object and purpose."

paragraphs.summary: Court states IRPA refugee provisions incorporate international convention; Vienna Convention Articles 31 and 32 guide treaty interpretation.

propositions.text: Supreme Court accepted Article 32 Vienna Convention to interpret Article 1F(c) Refugee Convention in Pushpanathan.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court of Canada accepted the applicability of Article 32 of the Vienna Convention to assist in the interpretation of Article 1F(c) of the Refugee Convention in accordance with section 98 exclusion in the Pushpanathan case.18

propositions.text: Supreme Court considered Convention on the Rights of the Child in Baker for permanent residency humanitarian grounds.
propositions.quote: The issue of Canada's international obligations under the Convention on the Rights of the Child for purposes of deciding applications for permanent residency on humanitarian and compassionate grounds was considered by the Supreme Court of Canada in the Baker decision.19

propositions.text: International treaties not part of Canadian law unless implemented by statute; values inform statutory interpretation.
propositions.quote: The Court followed previous jurisprudence in holding that international treaties do not form part of Canadian law, unless expressly implemented by statute. Notwithstanding this conclusion, the Court held that the values found in international human rights law can help to inform a contextual approach to statutory interpretation.

propositions.text: Convention on the Rights of the Child principles may inform humanitarian and compassionate interpretation when children involved.
propositions.quote: For this reason, the underlying principles of the Convention on the Rights of the Child may be used for purposes of interpreting the content of humanitarian and compassionate considerations when children are involved.

paragraphs.summary: Supreme Court accepted Vienna Convention Article 32 in Pushpanathan; held treaties not law unless statutory; values inform interpretation; CRC principles inform humanitarian grounds.

propositions.text: Supreme Court requires ambiguities from refugee convention incorporation be considered in light of IRPA objectives and international refugee and human rights law.
propositions.quote: Supreme Court of Canada jurisprudence requires that ambiguities arising from the incorporation of Canada's obligation under the 1951 Convention regarding the status of refugees be considered in light of the objectives of IPRA and within the broader context of international refugee and human rights law.

paragraphs.summary: Supreme Court requires ambiguities from refugee convention incorporation be considered in light of IRPA objectives and international refugee and human rights law.

propositions.text: IRPA subsection 3(2) outlines refugee objectives: saving lives, fulfilling international obligations, and denying access to security risks.
propositions.quote: Subsection 3(2) of the IRPA outlines the Act's objectives with respect to refugees: a) to recognize that the refugee program is in the first instance about saving lives and offering protection to the displaced and persecuted; (b) to fulfil Canada's international legal obligations with respect to refugees and affirm Canada's commitment to international efforts to provide assistance to those in need of resettlement; (h) to promote international justice and security by denying access to Canadian territory to persons, including refugee claimants, who are security risks or serious criminals.

paragraphs.summary: IRPA subsection 3(2) sets refugee objectives: saving lives, fulfilling international obligations, and denying access to security risks and serious criminals.

propositions.text: Article 1F(b) exclusion concerns serious non-political crimes before admission, part of international refugee law.
propositions.quote: Article 1F(b) exclusion concerns whether there are serious reasons for considering that the person committed a serious non-political crime prior to admission to the country. This concerns international refugee law as incorporated into the IRPA, not strictly one of Canadian criminal law.

propositions.text: International refugee law permits asylum-seekers to travel with fraudulent documents directly to asylum country without criminal charges if they report promptly and explain.
propositions.quote: International refugee law permits an asylum-seeker to travel with fraudulent documents directly to a country of asylum without risk of facing criminal charges, provided that the person reports to authorities and provides an adequate explanation for the necessity of having done so.

paragraphs.summary: Article 1F(b) exclusion concerns serious crimes pre-admission under international refugee law; asylum-seekers may use fraudulent documents if reporting promptly with explanation.

propositions.text: Article 31 Refugee Convention prohibits penalties for illegal entry if refugees come directly from threatened territory and report promptly with good cause.
propositions.quote: Article 31 of the Refugee Convention provides the following: 1. The Contracting States shall not impose penalties, on account of their illegal entry or presence, on refugees who, coming directly from a territory where their life or freedom was threatened in the sense of article 1, enter or are present in their territory without authorization, provided they present themselves without delay to the authorities and show good cause for their illegal entry or presence.

paragraphs.summary: Article 31 Refugee Convention prohibits penalties for illegal entry if refugees come directly from threatened territory and report promptly with good cause.

propositions.text: Goodwin-Gill analyzed drafting and implementation of Article 31, noting concerns about asylum shopping and secondary relocation.
propositions.quote: Guy Goodwin-Gill has provided a detailed assessment of the drafting history and national implementation of this article.20 Discussions among the State parties and in proposals found in the travaux préparatoires show that the State parties were concerned about asylum shopping and the secondary relocation of those who had been determined to be Convention refugees.

propositions.text: Transit countries can be included in 'coming directly' if asylum-seeker shows risk or lack of temporary protection there.
propositions.quote: If an asylum-seeker passes through third countries without legal documentation before arriving in the country of asylum, good reasons must be provided promptly as to why they were either at risk in the transit countries or they could not have obtained temporary protection in any of them.

propositions.text: Phrase 'coming directly' includes transit countries and allows passage through countries without temporary asylum.
propositions.quote: The phrase "coming directly from a territory in which life or freedom was threatened" can include a transit country, and allows for passage through countries in which temporary asylum is not available.

propositions.text: Section 133 in IRPA qualifies travel as direct or indirect.
propositions.quote: This is reflected in the wording of section 133 in IRPA that qualifies that the travel can be either direct or indirect.

propositions.text: Goodwin-Gill argues 'directly' should be assessed contextually including risk at trip stages.
propositions.quote: Goodwin-Gill argues that the term "directly" should not be strictly construed, but should be assessed in light of all of the relevant facts of the case, including the question of risk at various stages of the trip.

propositions.text: Good cause includes asylum-seeker's understanding, lack of knowledge, or third party instructions.
propositions.quote: "Good cause" can include the asylum-seekers understanding of the situation, lack of knowledge of procedures, or actions or instructions from a third party.

propositions.text: Penalties for illegal entry without regard to claim merits violate human rights obligations under ICCPR and regional instruments.
propositions.quote: He also submits that to impose penalties for illegal entry without regard to merits of the claim would violate human rights obligations under the International Convention on Civil and Political Rights, as well as regional human rights instruments.

propositions.text: Term 'penalties' not defined but appears to include prosecution, fines, imprisonment, or administrative detention not required.
propositions.quote: Goodwin-Gill notes that the term "penalties" is not defined, but appears to refer to prosecution, fine and imprisonment or administrative detention that is not required.22

paragraphs.summary: Goodwin-Gill analyzed Article 31, noting asylum shopping concerns; 'coming directly' includes transit countries; 'good cause' includes understanding; penalties violate human rights; 'penalties' include prosecution.

propositions.text: Article 31 drafting history shows focus on penalties for asylum seekers arriving without legal documents, not on criminality of conduct.
propositions.quote: The drafting history of Article 31 of the Refugee Convention shows that the State parties were dealing with the question of prosecution under domestic law of asylum seekers who arrived without legal documentation.

propositions.text: Article 31 aims to provide immunity from prosecution, not a defence against criminal culpability.
propositions.quote: the purpose of Article 31 was not to serve as a defence against criminal culpability, but rather to afford immunity from prosecution for a criminal offence.

propositions.text: Article 31 does not say a refugee using a forged passport is not guilty, but states the State should refrain from prosecuting if a good explanation is given.
propositions.quote: The article does not stipulate that a refugee who enters a country with a forged passport is not guilty of the offence, but rather that the State should refrain from prosecuting the individual, if a good explanation for the conduct can be provided.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Article 31's drafting history and purpose: it provides immunity from prosecution, not a defence, for asylum seekers arriving without legal documents.

propositions.text: Legal defences address whether a criminal act was committed; immunity from prosecution means policy weighs against charges, not that conduct was legal.
propositions.quote: Legal defences are relevant to the question of whether a criminal act was committed. Immunity from prosecution does not imply that the conduct was not illegal, but rather that public policy considerations weigh against proceeding with charges.

propositions.text: Section 133 IRPA prohibits charging asylum seekers for false documents while claim is pending, limited to prosecution in Canada.
propositions.quote: Section 133 of the IRPA is preceded by the rubric "Prosecution of Offences." It specifies that asylum-seekers may not be charged with an offence in relation to the coming into Canada with false documents, pending the outcome of the refugee claim.

propositions.text: Section 133 IRPA does not provide a defence entitling acquittal, only immunity from prosecution in Canada.
propositions.quote: It in no way provides a defence that would entitle an acquittal.

propositions.text: Federal Court decisions show immunity is relevant to equivalency of offences but not to whether a past offence was committed for article 1F(b) exclusion.
propositions.quote: This perspective is reflected in the Federal Court decisions that have been previously discussed... immunity from prosecution is a relevant factor to consider in establishing an equivalency between the two offences, even though it does not concern a legal defence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains immunity from prosecution under section 133 IRPA is limited and does not equate to a legal defence or negate past offences for exclusion.

propositions.text: Parties erred by confusing immunity from prosecution with legal defences in article 1F(b) exclusion context.
propositions.quote: The legal error that the parties made in the case under appeal lies in confusing immunities with defences.

propositions.text: Article 1F(b) exclusion concerns whether claimant committed serious non-political crimes before admission.
propositions.quote: Article 1F(b) exclusion concerns whether the claimant committed serious non- political crimes prior to admission to the country of refuge.

propositions.text: Personation and forged passport use are serious crimes under Canadian Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: Personation and use of a forged passport are serious crimes from the perspective of the Criminal Code of Canada.

propositions.text: Section 133 IRPA cannot serve as a defence negating commission of offence; it concerns prosecution in Canada only.
propositions.quote: Section 133 cannot serve as a defence that could lead to the conclusion that no offence was committed. The language of this section concerns the prosecution in Canada of those who are physically present in the country, not to whether document fraud is a serious criminal offence.

propositions.text: RPD erred by concluding Jayasekara/Febles factors need not be considered because no offence was committed.
propositions.quote: The RPD erred in concluding that the Jayasekara/ Febles factors did not need to be considered because no offence had been committed.

propositions.text: Correct legal approach requires article 1F(b) exclusion assessment using Federal Court of Appeal and Supreme Court mandated factors.
propositions.quote: The correct legal approach would have been to conduct an article 1F(b) exclusion assessment on the basis of the factors mandated by the Federal Court of Appeal, as affirmed by the Supreme Court of Canada.

propositions.text: Discussion of IRPA section 133 may be relevant as mitigating circumstances context.
propositions.quote: A discussion of IRPA section 133 could have taken place in the context of mitigating circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds parties erred by confusing immunity with defence; RPD erred by not applying mandated article 1F(b) factors and misapplying section 133 IRPA.

propositions.text: RPD alternatively concluded conduct was not serious for exclusion but gave no reasons or Jayasekara analysis.
propositions.quote: In the alternative, the RPD noted that, even if section 133 did not apply to absolve the Respondent from criminal culpability, the particular facts of the case lead to the conclusion that her conduct cannot be characterized as being serious for purposes of exclusion. No reasons were given and no Jayeasakara analysis was conducted.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes RPD alternatively found conduct not serious for exclusion but failed to provide reasons or conduct required analysis.

propositions.text: RAD reviews RPD decisions on correctness and can correct and re-determine unless new evidence needed.
propositions.quote: The RAD has a mandate to review RPD decision on the basis of correctness, and to correct and re-determine the case, unless evidence would need to be heard by the RPD.

propositions.text: Parties agree on underlying facts about forged passport use.
propositions.quote: In this case, the parties agree to the underlying facts with respect to the use of the forged passport.

propositions.text: Issue is correct interpretation and application of law regarding forged passport and exclusion.
propositions.quote: The issue is the correct interpretation and application of the law.

propositions.text: Independent review concludes RPD did not err in finding conduct not sufficiently serious to warrant exclusion.
propositions.quote: My independent review of the appeal leads me to conclude that the RPD did not err in its conclusion that the Respondent's conduct is not sufficiently serious to warrant exclusion from refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains RAD's review mandate, notes parties agree on facts, and concludes RPD did not err in finding conduct not serious enough for exclusion.

propositions.text: Respondent submits RPD failed to assess claim per Jayasekara/Febles factors and failed to consider conduct as mitigating factor.
propositions.quote: After submitting that no crime was committed by virtue of section 133 of the IRPA, the Respondent submits in the alternative that the RPD failed to assess the claim in accordance with the Jayasekara/Febles factors.

propositions.text: Respondent cites Federal Court Tabagua decision supporting failure to consider conduct as mitigating factor.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court Tabagua decision is cited in support of the submission that the RPD failed to consider her conduct as a mitigating factor in this assessment.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Respondent's submission that RPD failed to consider Jayasekara/Febles factors properly.
propositions.quote: I agree with this submission.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues RPD failed to assess claim per Jayasekara/Febles factors; the court agrees with this submission.

propositions.text: Respondent admitted conduct meets basic elements of crimes under sections 403 and 57 of CCC.
propositions.quote: The Respondent has admitted to have engaged in conduct that meets the basic elements of the crime.

propositions.text: Respondent fraudulently personated a Canadian citizen to avoid IRPA provisions and knew passport was forged.
propositions.quote: she fraudulently personated a Canadian citizen with the intent "to avoid arrest or prosecution or to obstruct, prevent or defeat the course of justice."... she knew that the passport was forged and used it in an attempt to cause others to deal with it as if it were genuine.

propositions.text: Sections 57 and 403 CCC elements apply to Respondent's conduct.
propositions.quote: The elements of the crimes described in sections 57 and 403 of the CCC apply to the Respondent.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the respondent admitted conduct meets elements of crimes under sections 403 and 57 of the Criminal Code of Canada.

propositions.text: Use of forged passport under section 57 CCC is indictable only; personation under section 403 CCC is hybrid offence.
propositions.quote: The use of a forged passport under section 57 of the CCC is prosecuted by means of indictment only. Personation pursuant to section 403 of the CCC is a hybrid offence that can be prosecuted either as a summary conviction offence or as an indictable offence.

propositions.text: CCC treats use of forged passport more seriously than identity fraud, both procedurally and in maximum sentence.
propositions.quote: Of the two, the CCC treats the use of a forged passport more seriously than identity fraud, both procedurally and with respect to the maximum sentence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the mode of prosecution and seriousness of offences under sections 57 and 403 CCC, with forged passport use treated more seriously.

propositions.text: Passport fraud under section 57 CCC punishable by imprisonment up to 14 years; personation up to 10 years if indictable.
propositions.quote: Passport fraud under section 57 is punishable with imprisonment not exceeding fourteen years. Personation can result in a term of imprisonment not exceeding ten years if it is prosecuted as an indictable offence.

propositions.text: CCC treats use of forged passport more seriously than identity fraud, both procedurally and in maximum sentence.
propositions.quote: Of the two, the CCC treats the use of a forged passport more seriously than identity fraud, both procedurally and with respect to the maximum sentence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states penalties for passport fraud and personation, noting forged passport use is treated more seriously.

propositions.text: RPD accepted Respondent used forged passport solely to make refugee claim in Canada.
propositions.quote: The RPD accepted as being true that the Respondent obtained and used the forged Canadian passport for the sole purpose of making a refugee claim in Canada.

propositions.text: Court has no reason to doubt RPD's credibility assessment on this fact.
propositions.quote: In light of the preceding credibility assessment, I have no good reason to doubt this.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found and the court accepts that the respondent used the forged passport solely to make a refugee claim in Canada.

propositions.text: Section 133 is one factor in assessing crime seriousness for Article 1F(b) exclusion.
propositions.quote: Section 133 is one factor among others that can be taken into consideration with respect to the seriousness of the crime for purposes of Article 1F(b) exclusion.

propositions.text: IRPA subsection 3(2) paragraphs (g) and (h) outline refugee protection goals: safety/security and denying serious criminals entry.
propositions.quote: Subsection 3(2) of the IRPA at paragraphs (g) and (h) outlines two of the objectives of the Act with respect to refugees. The first goal is to protect the safety and security of Canadian society, and the second is to deny entry to serious criminals or security risks in order to promote international justice and security.

propositions.text: These goals must be pursued respecting Canada's international legal obligations.
propositions.quote: Paragraph (b) requires that this be done in the context of respect for Canada's international legal obligations.

paragraphs.summary: The court states section 133 is a factor in assessing crime seriousness, and IRPA goals include safety and respecting international obligations.

propositions.text: International refugee law allows asylum seekers to use false travel documents to seek asylum in safe third countries, with some allowances.
propositions.quote: international refugee law allows asylum-seekers to make use of false travel documents in order to seek asylum in a safe third country. Although travel must be direct, allowances are made for passage through unsafe counties or those in which refugee protection is not reasonably available.

propositions.text: Canada's section 133 IRPA extends this principle to allow indirect travel with false documents.
propositions.quote: Canada extended this principle in section 133 of the IRPA to allow for indirect travel.

propositions.text: Section 133 is not directly applicable to Article 1F(b) exclusion but indicates travel with false documents for asylum is not a serious offence.
propositions.quote: Although this provision is not directly applicable to Article 1F(b) exclusion, the international human rights context indicates that travel with false travel documents for the purpose of seeking asylum is not a serious offence.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains international law and section 133 IRPA allow false travel documents for asylum, indicating such travel is not a serious offence for exclusion.

propositions.text: UNHCR Handbook states serious non-political crimes must be capital or very grave punishable acts; minor crimes insufficient.
propositions.quote: The UNHCR Refugee Status Determination Handbook notes that it is difficult to define what a serious non-political crime is for purposes of exclusion. Minor crimes punishable by moderate sentences do not suffice. They must either be a capital crime or a "very grave punishable act."

propositions.text: Aggravating circumstances like prior convictions may be considered in assessing seriousness.
propositions.quote: Aggravating circumstances such as previous criminal convictions may be taken into account.

propositions.text: Some crimes committed to flee persecution may be overlooked; severity of crime affects acceptability.
propositions.quote: The UNHCR Handbook notes at paragraph 158 that some crimes may be committed in order for a refugee to leave the country of persecution. For example, it may be possible to overlook crashing a stolen car through border control, but it becomes more difficult to accept if an asylum-seeker hijacks an aircraft.

paragraphs.summary: The UNHCR Handbook explains serious non-political crimes must be very grave; some crimes to flee persecution may be overlooked depending on severity.

propositions.text: Respondent has no criminal record and used one forged document to seek asylum, posing no danger to public or security.
propositions.quote: The Respondent has no criminal record and made use of one forged travel document in an attempt to seek asylum in Canada. She does not pose a danger to the public, nor to the security of Canada.

propositions.text: Respondent committed offence to flee persecution but lacked truthfulness about forged passport, which is aggravating.
propositions.quote: She committed the offence in order to flee persecution. However, her lack of truthfulness about the false passport is an aggravating factor.

propositions.text: Respondent did not disclose forged passport use until confronted, despite lawyer assistance, violating Article 31 principle.
propositions.quote: The Respondent did not disclose the use of the forged passport until confronted by the CBSA, despite the assistance of a lawyer. The principle behind the immunity from prosecution under the Refugee Convention requires that one disclose the illegal conduct promptly to authorities and to provide a reasonable explanation at that time.

propositions.text: Failure to report promptly is an aggravating factor in international law context, though not directly applicable here.
propositions.quote: Although not directly applicable, the fact that she failed to respect the obligation to report is an aggravating factor in the context of international law.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondent has no criminal record, used forged document to flee persecution, but failed to disclose promptly, an aggravating factor.

propositions.text: Parties did not cite Canadian case law on sentencing of similarly situated persons.
propositions.quote: The parties did not cite Canadian case law with respect to the way Canadian criminal courts have sentenced similarly-situated persons.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes parties did not cite Canadian case law on sentencing for similar offences.

propositions.text: Considering mitigating/aggravating factors and international law, offence not serious enough for Article 1F(b) exclusion.
propositions.quote: When the mitigating and aggravating factors are considered in light international refugee and human rights law principles and in the context of the Jayasekara/ Febles factors, I conclude that the offence committed is not sufficiently serious to warrant exclusion under Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention.

propositions.text: If forged passport used for other purposes, facts would determine seriousness for exclusion.
propositions.quote: If a forged passport were used for purposes other than to seek asylum in Canada, the particular facts of the case would need to be considered in order to determine the seriousness of the offence.

propositions.text: Here, purpose of use determines offence not serious enough for exclusion.
propositions.quote: In the case under appeal, the purpose for which it was used is determinative of the conclusion that it was not sufficiently serious to warrant exclusion from refugee protection.

propositions.text: Minister correct that section 133 immunity not directly applicable, especially given failure to disclose truth timely.
propositions.quote: Although the Minister is correct that section 133 immunity is not directly applicable to the Respondent's situation, especially given that fact that she did not disclose the truth in a timely manner as required by Article 31 of the Refugee Convention,

propositions.text: Underlying principle of section 133 supports conclusion offence not serious enough for exclusion.
propositions.quote: the underlying principle supports the conclusion that this offence is not of sufficiently serious nature to warrant exclusion.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the offence is not serious enough for exclusion, with purpose of use determinative, despite section 133 immunity not directly applying.

propositions.text: Despite RPD's failure to conduct mandated assessment, court agrees with its final determination.
propositions.quote: Despite my conclusion that the RPD erred in its failure to conduct an assessment using the legally-mandated factors, I agree with its final determination.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with RPD's final determination despite its failure to conduct the mandated assessment.

propositions.text: Minister argues RPD erred by not considering Respondent's lack of honesty in credibility assessment and misinterpreting section 133 IRPA.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Minister that the RPD erred by failing to take the Respondent's lack of honesty about the forged passport into consideration in the credibility assessment. In addition, the RPD erred in misinterpreting the applicability of section 133 of the IRPA and by failing to conduct a Jayasekara/ Febles assessment as it was required to do.

propositions.text: Court concurs RPD erred on section 133 and credibility but finds Respondent's past persecution claim likely true and conduct not warranting exclusion.
propositions.quote: Although I agree with the Minister that the RPD erred in its treatment of section 133 and in its failure to consider the Respondent's lack of truthfulness in its credibility assessment, I concur with the outcome.

paragraphs.summary: The Minister argues RPD erred on honesty and section 133; the court agrees on errors but concurs with the outcome.

propositions.text: Despite RPD's mistakes, conclusion that Respondent is a Convention refugee not excluded under Article 1F(b) is correct.
propositions.quote: Despite the mistakes made by the RPD, the conclusion that the Respondent is a Convention refugee who is not excluded from protection by operation of Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention is correct.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes that despite RPD's mistakes, the respondent is correctly found a Convention refugee not excluded under Article 1F(b).

propositions.text: RAD dismisses appeal and confirms RPD decision that appellant is a Convention refugee not excluded under Article 1F(b).
propositions.quote: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is a Convention refugee who is not excluded from refugee protection by operation of Article 1F(b) of the Refugee Convention, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the appellant is a Convention refugee not excluded under Article 1F(b).
